title: When Your Animation Tears the Fabric: An Interview with 3D Creator UBASM
content:
## ![](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202601/04a9f0c3388441e4b25c6b4a8049fcc6/images/e4ee5582756441b9ad344788e009a23cUserspotlight_Jan.png)![](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202601/04a9f0c3388441e4b25c6b4a8049fcc6/images/ae1f969af6924e40bba3021abe21b8f2cvl_512.gif)**_What happens when your digital garment animation is so powerful it literally tears the fabric apart?_**

![9338236f76b947628ddef930062d5ac2](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202601/04a9f0c3388441e4b25c6b4a8049fcc6/images/9338236f76b947628ddef930062d5ac2Kolon%20reels%20combined%20resized.gif)

_That’s just one of the challenges UBASM—the creative mind behind the CLO 2025.2 release artwork—solved while bringing the 'Perfect Home: SOS' concept to life. In partnership with internationally acclaimed artist Do Ho Suh and Kolon Sport, he created a wearable shelter designed to protect the human body in extreme environments._

_In our latest interview, he reveals the clever keyframing technique he developed to achieve controlled inflation and shares the secrets behind his distinct artistic vision. Discover how mastering the technical side of CLO helped him build an incredible portfolio and find his own creative voice._

_![ebe0e5b3c01a499fa33c30816f5d1561](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202601/04a9f0c3388441e4b25c6b4a8049fcc6/images/ebe0e5b3c01a499fa33c30816f5d1561release25_2_cvl_en.png)"Recognize this masterpiece? The official CLO 2025.2 release artwork, created by UBASM."_

  
**Welcome, UBASM! It’s a pleasure to feature your work. Before we dive into your design process, we have to ask about your unique alias: 'UBASM' (Undercover Banana and Spacemonkey). What’s the story behind it?**

I wanted something playful, a reminder not to take life too seriously, because it’s way too short for that.

**To start, could you walk us through your journey into the world of 3D art? What first drew you to this field, and how did CLO become a central tool for building and shaping your creative portfolio?**

I first began my journey by creating digital-only fashion. The work of artists like Antoni Tudisco, Soze, and studios like The Fabricant drew me into it, and I immediately fell in love with its limitless possibilities. Fashion became my medium for artistic expression, and 3D tools opened up a new space for experimentation.  
What fascinated me most was the magic of cloth simulation, watching digital garments behave like real fabric felt really satisfying. I also loved the challenge of achieving photorealistic results, working with fibers, textures, and hair systems to blur the line between the digital and the real. CLO became central to my process because of its powerful simulation tools and flexibility.  


![0b731ff1f6014387a6d8c7265af674c7](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202601/04a9f0c3388441e4b25c6b4a8049fcc6/images/0b731ff1f6014387a6d8c7265af674c7THUMB_V1.jpg)

**Let's talk about your recent project with Kolon Sport. This wasn't just a garment; it was a "wearable home" concept. Could you tell us about your specific role in this unique collaboration? What were the challenges of animating such a complex structure, and how did you leverage CLO to ensure the movement felt realistic?**

As part of Do Ho Suh Studio’s collaboration with Kolon Sport, I was responsible for animating the survival suit in CLO3D. The main challenge was achieving controlled inflation within CLO3D. A single, instant inflation didn’t work because the force was so extreme that it tore the mesh apart. To solve this, I keyframed the inflation to control the process more precisely, by increasing the pressure by about 10% every 10 frames. It required a lot of fine-tuning since the suit had multiple inflatable sections, each reacting differently and needing its own frame-to-pressure ratio. In the end, the method worked really well. By adjusting those ratios, I could present the client with various inflation speeds and fabric behaviors.

![cceb7cb4ba4d46ebafe9c23193c53e5c](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202601/04a9f0c3388441e4b25c6b4a8049fcc6/images/cceb7cb4ba4d46ebafe9c23193c53e5cHAMMER05.jpg)  
_“Wearable Architecture: The 'SOS' suit transforms from a garment into a personal shelter. UBASM used CLO's pressure settings to animate this metamorphosis smoothly without breaking the intricate mesh structure.”_

![90e79a521c4441308c6b93805ec5f15d](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202601/04a9f0c3388441e4b25c6b4a8049fcc6/images/90e79a521c4441308c6b93805ec5f15dHAMMER04.jpg)

**Collaboration is a huge part of the creative industry. You’ve worked with both brands and other 3D artists. How does your creative process adapt when collaborating? What do you see as the key to successfully merging your artistic style with a brand's identity or another creator's vision?**

Collaborating with other artists gives me the chance to get new perspectives during the process. When you create on your own, it’s easy to develop blind spots, so getting thoughtful feedback helps push me beyond boundaries and grow. When it comes to blending my artistic style with a brand’s identity or another creator’s vision, I believe the key is to always kind of keep ‘designing for yourself’. They reached out because they connected with my way of seeing things, so staying close to that intuition usually leads to the most authentic result for me.

![444ce3aed7e846eb94d5ae3aca2a18a7](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202601/04a9f0c3388441e4b25c6b4a8049fcc6/images/444ce3aed7e846eb94d5ae3aca2a18a7image%20%2876%29.png)  
**Beyond CLO, what other tools are essential to your workflow (for rendering, modeling, post-production, etc.), and how do you create synergy between them and CLO?**

These days, I mainly use Houdini, which pairs really well with CLO3D. I often export Alembic files from CLO and bring them into Houdini, where I refine and optimize the sim using Vellum. That extra layer of simulation allows me to push the realism further.

  
**Thinking about your recent work, could you share a personal project that you’re particularly proud of? What was the core concept behind it, and which CLO features were most essential in bringing that specific vision to life? Perhaps there was a particular tool or technique that was key to achieving the final look?**

Last year, I created a project called “Modern Hues” (<https://www.behance.net/gallery/215878047/Modern-Hues>) which I’m proud of. The core concept was about how digital fashion can give everyone the freedom to tell their story through color, texture, and form. It became an exploration of individuality and self-expression, using vibrant palettes and bold shapes to reflect different identities. In terms of CLO features, I had a lot of fun working with inflatable and puffed-up fabric techniques. CLO makes it very intuitive to experiment with volume, almost like sculpting with fabric, which was essential to achieving the final look.

![be12d13e822340d3bf67f491cb7bd211](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202601/04a9f0c3388441e4b25c6b4a8049fcc6/images/be12d13e822340d3bf67f491cb7bd211merged-image-mergeimagesonline.com.png)

**Your work has a distinct aesthetic. Where do you typically draw your inspiration from to create such unique visuals? Do you rely on mood boards, follow specific brands, or find ideas in other hobbies and interests like film, music, or nature?**

I keep a folder with thousands of photos and screenshots, from fashion shows to paintings, surreal objects, and anything else that has once made me feel something emotionally at some point. Alongside that, I keep a notes file filled with hundreds of little idea fragments. Whenever something comes to mind, I write it down immediately. Whenever I feel like I start to get tunnel vision, I revisit these folders and notes. I’ve probably only developed about 5% of those ideas, but I think that’s just the reality of working in 3D. At some point, you have to pick a direction and commit.  
One of the hardest parts is finding your own aesthetic. For me, it’s not something I can force or consciously direct, it just develops over time. I like to think I’m gradually finding mine.

  
**Every artist faces creative blocks or technical hurdles. Could you share a time you felt like giving up on a project? How did you overcome that challenge?**

For creative blocks, what works best for me is the idea of ‘killing your darlings’. It’s okay to let go of ideas and start over. More often than not, you’ve learned something valuable in the first attempt, and the second version turns out much stronger.  
When it comes to technical challenges, I’ve found that reaching out to the community helps a lot. In these cases I just post about issues on Instagram stories, asking if anyone has tips or tricks. The CLO community is super supportive.

  
**Finally, for the many aspiring 3D artists in our community who are just starting their journey, what is one key piece of advice you would give them for using CLO to build a strong portfolio and develop their own unique creative voice?**

I would say: don’t ignore the technical side. It might not give you instant results, but developing a broad set of skills in CLO3D really expands your creative range. At least for me this has always worked, learning new techniques spark so many new ideas, often more than anything else.

  
**Looking ahead, what is a "dream project" you hope to tackle as an artist?**

For me, the dream project isn’t necessarily about a specific brand or collab, it’s more about finding my own style that feels completely natural, like being a fish in water. I want to discover my own unique way of expressing fashion through creative uses of design and tech (by combining garments with sims, forms, and organic elements inspired by nature). It might sound a bit abstract because I’m still in the process of exploring it, but in short: my dream project is to really find my own aesthetic.
content_description: Explore the innovative fusion of digital garment animation and wearable architecture through UBASM’s creative process and groundbreaking use of CLO3D in the ‘Perfect Home: SOS’ survival suit project.

title: Desperately Need Better 2D Production Tools
content:
![](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202601/2542f35a35794a868606fb0aa376eb6c/images/79a0215c7c7f435b8660bbd314a878efIMG_0501.jpeg)To the CLO Dev Team,

I am writing this out of genuine frustration because I love the 3D visualization capabilities of this software, but the 2D side is becoming a massive bottleneck. I want to rely on CLO as my sole tool for pattern making, but right now, **the production workflow feels broken.**

We have enough 3D texture features. Please, I am begging you to focus on the "boring" but essential problems that allow us to actually manufacture clothes.

Here are the three specific areas where the workflow is currently agonizing for production:

**1\. The "Global Grading" Nightmare** Grading in CLO feels incredibly clunky. Currently, the grading logic is too interconnected.

  * **The Problem:** When I need to adjust a specific point on a larger size (ex; fixing a fit issue on a Size XL), it often shifts the geometry of the Base Size or the entire nest.

  * **The Workaround:** I am currently forced to save _independent files_ for every single size just to keep them safe. This defeats the entire purpose of using CAD software.

  * **The Request:** We need a robust "Non-Proportional" or "Break Link" grading feature where I can manipulate a specific size in the nest without it destroying the others.




**2\. The Annotation Tool is an Inconvenience**

Creating simple technical labels shouldn't be this hard. The current 2D Annotation tool is incredibly frustrating and lacks basic precision.

  * **The Input Box:** The typing box itself is unnecessarily difficult. It’s tiny, clunky to edit, and feels like an afterthought.

  * **The Request:** Please overhaul the UI for annotations. We need a properties panel where we can set all the needs of a pattern information text without fighting the interface.




**3\. SVG Export from Print Layout (The Waste Reduction Issue)** This is a huge pain point for those of us printing our own patterns.

  * **The Problem:** I use the "Print Layout" mode to nest my patterns and minimize fabric waste. However, I cannot export this optimized layout as a vector file (SVG). I can only view it or save images.

  * **The Request:** Please allow us to **Export to SVG directly from the Print Layout view.** I need the vector data of my nested marker so I can actually print the patterns efficiently without wasting paper or fabric.




**Conclusion** I want to use CLO for everything, but right now, the 2D tools feel like a struggle. I don’t want to hop back and forth between softwares.

### Community Post Comments:
Comment 1: Hi There. Thank you for the post. It looks like you do not have an active CLO account attached to the account. Can you please let us know what you CLO account name is? Thank you 🙂We do always recommend posting questions using the account that is attached to your active CLO subscription
content_description: A user feedback page highlighting critical 2D workflow improvements needed in CLO software to enhance pattern making, grading, annotation, and export features for efficient garment production.

title: Pairing Avatar With Graded Size
content:
Pairing Avatar With Graded Size

Let’s say

Step 1) I created a Custom Avatar (Base Custom Avatar) which I chose a default avatar in the size of 46 and modified It for increasing the Belly and Hips measurements.

Step 2) I created a Sewing Pattern for this Custom Avatar. (Base Custom Avatar)

Step 3) Then we graded this Sewing Pattern.

Step 4) Now I want to see the Graded Versions of the pattern on my Custom Avatar but in this time in “the different sizes”.

Question 1) Now do we have to create the different size versions of my Custom Base Avatar or

does Clo3D create different size versions of my Custom Base Avatar automatically?

Question 2) Let’s say we create the different size versions of my Custom Base Avatar.

Is this way alright?

Q2 Step 1) Let’s say we chose the size 46 of the Default Clo3D Avatar for creating my Custom Base Avatar.

Then I applied these modifications;

(and I note these=

Chest : -5 cm

Waist : +10 cm

Hips : +5cm

Thighs : +3cm

Q2 Step 2) Now I want to create the size 44 version of my Custom Base Avatar.

So I chose the size 44 of the Default Clo3D this time.

and apply the exact modifications to this particular default avatar. (the Size 44)

Chest : -5 cm

Waist : +10 cm

Hips : +5cm

Thighs : +3cm

and I get the size 44 version of my Custom Avatar.

Is this method alright?

Any Suggestions?

### Community Post Comments:
Comment 1: This is how I do it : if your base size is a custom avatar ( like CLO avatar size 44 but chest -5cm) and you other sizes are also different for the CLO avatars sizes , for example CLO avatar size 42 with also chest -5cm. then you have to create these custom avatars for each size first and save each size as a .avs file. I try to find a CLO avatar size as close as possible and change that one. In your projectfile with the graded pattern you pair these .avs custom made avatar sizes to the corresponding graded size. I do find that it is not always stable, I have had files with grading and paired avatars that when I opened files after a time, the file lost the paired avatars and I had to pair them again. Hope this will help :)

Comment 2: Hi, if your custom sizes diverge from the CLO default sizes, you have to create new size sets for all the different sizes you wish to check the graded fit on.
Reply 1: How? Like the one I had explained on my post? Can you check that please?
Reply 2: @wdeckers explained the way above - it is preferable to start from the default size that is already nearest to your own measurement chart, edit from there and save those sizes.
content_description: This page explores how to effectively pair custom avatars with graded sewing patterns in Clo3D by creating size-specific avatar versions to visualize pattern fit across different sizes.

title: Notches do not appear when exporting the pattern in PLT
content:
Download the latest version of CLO3D 2025.2.256 When I create a pattern and add notches, they appear in the pattern, but when I export the pattern in PLT format and open it in Illustrator, the pattern appears without the notches I had added (this never happened with previous versions). I don't know how to make the notches appear when I export the file.

title: Input fields don't save
content:
I'm using Clo3D 2025.2.256 and since this latest update, anything I type in input fields (like Name of a pattern piece) doesn't get saved. 

Steps to reproduce:

  1. Select a pattern piece

  2. Type anything like "Test" in the Name field of the pattern piece.

  3. Select another pattern piece

  4. Select the first pattern piece again.




Problem:

The entered name is not saved. Instead, the default/previous value is there again.

The same thing also happens in nearly all the input fields in the Print Layout "Nest Settings".

### Community Post Comments:
Comment 1: Hi bettina, the name field in the Print Layout is coming from the Fabric, not the pattern itself. I have also tried importing a PDF and changing the names, and it works for me as well. If the issue is still recurring for you, please contact our support team (https://connect.clo-set.com/community/post/7f64c10b03664d5288f8d8c6c13a5c52 and share as much information as possible (files, screenshots, video recording).

Comment 2: Hi there,Did you change the name of the pattern piece in the Property Editor? I've checked on my side and I didn't manage to recreate this issue whether it's with an imported pattern piece or a newly created one.
Reply 1: Hello, yes, that's exactly the field I'm talking about. I generally work with imported pattern pieces (via PDF import). Could you please also try going into the print layout and changing the width of a fabric there using the cm or mm input fields? That's where mine is broken most consistently.
content_description: This page aims to report and troubleshoot the issue where input field entries are not saved in Clo3D 2025.2.256, affecting pattern piece names and Print Layout settings.
